narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated an 82.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain; it means the estimated risk was high enough that the school chose not to offer admission.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You are in the first decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. Your first-year standing was the second most influential factor: you are also in the first decile there, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile. Your LSAT score of 28 was the third most important factor and is below the accepted-student average of about 37. All three of these academic indicators pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure rather than success, and together they outweighed other information in your profile.

To improve future chances, ask admissions for specific feedback, consider retaking the LSAT if you can prepare substantially, and strengthen your academic record through relevant coursework or a structured bar-readiness program. If your grades were affected by hardship, document that context. You may also apply to programs that review candidates more holistically, especially those that value work experience, personal circumstances, and a clear plan for bar preparation.
